Finn's bestselling novel, the experience is a claustrophobic slow-burn that trades on atmosphere and unreliable narration, building toward revelations designed to recontextualize everything that came before.

name: Barbie
description: Greta Gerwig transformed a plastic doll into a vehicle for genuine philosophical inquiry, creating an adventure fantasy comedy that is simultaneously a corporate product, a feminist statement, and a meditation on what it means to be human. Margot Robbie plays Stereotypical Barbie with radiant sincerity, her existential crisis triggered by sudden thoughts of death that send her tumbling from the pink perfection of Barbie Land into the messy, disappointing real world. Ryan Gosling's Ken — vacant, desperately seeking purpose, and gloriously committed to the bit — delivers one of the most unexpectedly layered comedic performances in recent memory. The production design is extraordinary, constructing Barbie Land as a practical-effects wonderland that makes artificiality itself beautiful. Gerwig and co-writer Noah Baumbach thread jokes about patriarchy, corporate feminism, and existential dread through a story that never loses its warmth or accessibility. America Ferrera's monologue about the impossible contradictions of womanhood became an instant cultural touchstone. The experience refuses to be just one thing — too smart for a toy commercial, too fun for a lecture, too sincere for pure satire. A phenomenon that proved audiences will show up in enormous numbers for stories that respect their intelligence while making them laugh.

name: Top Gun: Maverick
description: Tom Cruise delivered what many consider the definitive legacy sequel — a continuation that justifies its own existence by doing what its predecessor did, only better. Director Joseph Kosinski stages aerial combat sequences using real fighter jets with the actors inside them, and the difference between this and CGI-dependent spectacle is visceral and immediate. The action drama follows Pete Mitchell as he returns to the Top Gun program to train a new generation of pilots for an impossible mission, including Rooster, the son of his late wingman Goose, played by Miles Teller. The emotional core is surprisingly potent: Maverick's guilt, his refusal to let go of the cockpit, and his complicated responsibility toward a young man whose father's death he still carries. The flying sequences are breathtaking — shot with IMAX cameras strapped to F/A-18 cockpits, they deliver a physical sensation of speed, G-force, and spatial awareness that no amount of digital rendering can replicate. The supporting cast, including Jennifer Connelly and Jon Hamm, fills out a story that honors the original's tone without being trapped by it. A blockbuster that proves practical filmmaking at extreme scale can still generate genuine wonder.

name: Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny
description: Harrison Ford's final outing as the iconic archaeologist finds Indiana Jones in a world that has moved past him — the space race era, where former Nazis have been recruited by NASA and adventure feels like a relic. Director James Mangold takes the reins from Steven Spielberg for an action adventure that opens with a de-aged Ford in a spectacular World War II sequence before settling into a globe-trotting quest for the Antikythera mechanism, Archimedes' legendary device. Phoebe Waller-Bridge brings sharp energy as Helena Shaw, Indy's goddaughter and a morally flexible treasure hunter whose relationship with the aging hero provides both friction and warmth. Mads Mikkelsen plays the villain with quiet menace — a Nazi physicist whose obsession with the artifact drives the central conflict. The set pieces move through Moroccan markets, Mediterranean dive sites, and ancient ruins with the serial-adventure pacing the franchise is built on. The story grapples openly with aging and obsolescence in ways the earlier entries never needed to, giving Ford material that resonates beyond nostalgia. The experience carries the weight of finality, serving as both a farewell to a character and an acknowledgment that some adventures have natural endings.

name: Raya and the Last Dragon
description: Walt Disney Animation crafted a Southeast Asian-inspired fantasy that centers on a warrior's quest to reassemble a magical gem and restore trust to a fractured world, channeling themes of unity and faith into an action-packed animated adventure. Kelly Marie Tran voices Raya with fierce determination and guarded vulnerability — a lone warrior whose inability to trust anyone is both her greatest strength and the obstacle she must overcome. Awkwafina brings comic warmth to Sisu, the last surviving dragon, whose bubbly optimism clashes productively with Raya's hardened pragmatism. The animation is stunning, drawing from the landscapes, architecture, and martial arts traditions of Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia, and the Philippines to create a world that feels culturally grounded rather than generically exotic. The action sequences — particularly the hand-to-hand combat — are choreographed with a precision unusual for family animation, giving the fights real kinetic weight. The story's central argument is deceptively simple: that broken worlds are healed by choosing to trust even when trust has been repeatedly betrayed. The emotional stakes escalate toward a climax that demands genuine sacrifice, and the narrative earns its resolution by making that sacrifice feel costly rather than convenient.

name: The Flash
description: Ezra Miller stars as Barry Allen in DC's long-gestating attempt to bring the multiverse concept to its cinematic universe, as the speedster breaks the time barrier to save his mother and inadvertently fractures reality itself. Director Andy Muschietti builds an action adventure science fiction story around the emotional kernel of a son's grief, using Barry's desperate attempt to rewrite personal tragedy as the catalyst for universe-spanning consequences. The narrative sends Barry into an alternate timeline where he meets a younger version of himself and encounters Michael Keaton's Batman — a return that delivers genuine nostalgia and gives Keaton the kind of sendoff his iteration of the character never received. Sasha Calle debuts as Supergirl, bringing intensity to a story that otherwise leans heavily on humor and meta-references. The multiverse mechanics allow for cameos and visual spectacle that range from clever to overwhelming, and the CGI-heavy final act pushes the digital effects into territory that divided audiences. Beneath the blockbuster machinery, the story asks whether saving one person is worth unraveling everything else — a question it answers with surprising emotional directness. A flawed but ambitious swing at DC's most conceptually challenging character.

name: Vivo
description: Sony Pictures Animation and Lin-Manuel Miranda crafted this animated musical adventure about a kinkajou — a small, honey-loving rainforest mammal — who sets out on a cross-country journey to deliver a love song from his elderly musical partner to the woman who got away decades ago. Miranda's original songs blend Cuban musical traditions with contemporary pop sensibility, and the standout numbers carry an emotional specificity that elevates the story beyond its simple premise. The animation shifts between Havana's warm, saturated streetscapes and the wilds of the Florida Everglades, using visual style changes to mirror the tonal range of the music. Vivo himself, voiced with scrappy charm, is a performer whose world has shrunk to one stage and one partnership, making his reluctant journey into the wider world a story about letting go as much as holding on. The comedy finds a strong partner in Gabi, a young girl whose chaotic energy and punk-rock sensibility contrasts with Vivo's refined musicianship, creating a buddy dynamic that drives the narrative's middle stretch. The family-friendly surface conceals a surprisingly bittersweet core about missed connections, aging, and the songs that carry what words cannot.

name: Wicked
description: Jon M. Chu brings the beloved Broadway phenomenon to screen with Cynthia Erivo as Elphaba and Ariana Grande as Glinda, and the casting alone justifies the adaptation — Erivo's powerhouse vocals and raw emotional intensity paired with Grande's comedic precision and vocal agility create a dynamic that honors the stage production while finding its own register. The drama fantasy romance follows two women at Shiz University in the Land of Oz whose unlikely friendship forms across every conceivable divide — popularity, appearance, temperament, and ultimately moral conviction. The production design expands Oz into a fully realized world, with Emerald City rendered in art deco grandeur and the university campus given the texture of a lived-in institution rather than a stage set. Stephen Schwartz's iconic score translates powerfully, with "Defying Gravity" serving as the emotional and narrative crescendo. The story underneath the spectacle is about how societies create villains out of people who refuse to comply, and how the pressure to conform can fracture even the deepest bonds. The musical numbers are staged with cinematic ambition, using camera movement and scale in ways the stage cannot. A sweeping, emotionally charged experience built on two extraordinary performances.

name: Wish Dragon
description: Set in modern Shanghai, this animated fantasy adventure comedy follows Din, a working-class college student who accidentally summons Long, a wish-granting dragon trapped in a teapot for centuries, and uses his three wishes to reconnect with a childhood friend who has moved into a different social stratosphere. The story is essentially a contemporary retelling of Aladdin filtered through Chinese cultural sensibilities, but it finds its own voice through the specificity of its setting — the contrast between old Shanghai neighborhoods and gleaming skyscrapers, the pressure of economic mobility, and the way wealth reshapes friendships. John Cho voices Long with imperious charm, a dragon who has seen countless wish-makers squander their desires on predictable wants. The animation, produced by Sony Pictures Animation and Base FX, renders Shanghai with affectionate detail, and the action sequences involving rooftop chases and villainous henchmen bring kinetic family-friendly energy. The romance subplot is gentle and understated, and the comedy lands most effectively when exploring the culture shock of a Tang Dynasty dragon navigating modern technology. The emotional center is simpler than its fantasy trappings suggest: a story about realizing that the people you miss are worth more than the things you want.

name: Wonder Woman 1984
description: Patty Jenkins returns to direct Gal Gadot as Diana Prince in a sequel that trades the gritty World War I setting of the original for the neon excess of the 1980s, building an action adventure fantasy around a magical wishing stone that grants desires at devastating cost. Pedro Pascal plays Maxwell Lord, a charismatic con man whose wish for ultimate power sets off a global chain reaction, while Kristen Wiig transforms from a meek, overlooked scientist into the formidable Cheetah. The story leans into themes of longing, sacrifice, and the seductive danger of getting what you want, with Diana's impossible reunion with Steve Trevor — Chris Pine, charmingly out of time — providing the emotional backbone. The action sequences range from an elaborate mall heist to a desert convoy chase, staged with the kind of colorful, optimistic energy that distinguishes the DC Extended Universe's brightest corner. Jenkins' visual style embraces warmth and sincerity over darkness, making this one of the most tonally distinct superhero entries of its era. The narrative's ambition occasionally exceeds its execution, particularly in its globe-spanning third act, but Gadot's genuine warmth and the story's earnest belief in human goodness give it an identity that defies franchise formula.

name: Words on Bathroom Walls
description: Charlie Plummer stars as Adam, a high school senior navigating a schizophrenia diagnosis while trying to maintain a normal life — attending a new Catholic school, pursuing his dream of becoming a chef, and falling for Maya, a sharp, guarded classmate played by Taylor Russell. The drama romance distinguishes itself from typical mental health narratives by visualizing Adam's hallucinations as fully realized characters who occupy the frame alongside him, giving the audience direct access to his subjective experience rather than observing it from the outside. This choice transforms the story from a clinical portrait into something more intimate and occasionally surreal, as Adam negotiates with voices that feel as real to him as the people around him. The tone balances genuine humor with stretches of real anguish, never romanticizing the condition but refusing to reduce Adam to his diagnosis. Russell's Maya is written as a person with her own pressures and secrets rather than a redemptive love interest, and their chemistry grounds the story in something recognizably human. Walton Goggins appears as a supportive stepfather whose quiet decency provides emotional stability. A tender, specific story about the gap between the self others see and the self you experience from the inside.

name: Ava
description: Jessica Chastain plays the title character in this action crime thriller about a black ops assassin whose perfectly compartmentalized life begins unraveling when a botched job puts her on her own organization's kill list. Director Tate Taylor surrounds Chastain with a supporting cast that includes John Malkovich as her mentor and handler, Colin Farrell as the cold-blooded operative sent to eliminate her, and Common as an ex-boyfriend caught in the crossfire. The story follows familiar beats of the rogue-agent genre — the trained killer discovering she is now the target — but Chastain's commitment to the physicality of the role and the character's recovery from addiction add texture to what could otherwise feel routine. The fight choreography is efficient and grounded rather than stylized, prioritizing brutal practicality over elegance. The thriller elements build as Ava's professional and personal worlds collide, with family dynamics adding a layer of emotional complexity to the standard betrayal-and-survival framework. The pacing moves briskly through European locations and domestic confrontations, though the narrative occasionally struggles to balance its assassin-on-the-run mechanics with its more introspective character work. A competent genre exercise elevated by its lead performance.

name: The French Dispatch
description: Wes Anderson's love letter to journalism — specifically to The New Yorker and the vanishing tradition of long-form magazine writing — takes the form of an anthology structured as the final issue of a fictional American magazine published in a fictional French city. The comedy drama features three distinct stories: an imprisoned artist whose work becomes a sensation, a student revolution told through the eyes of a detached journalist, and a kidnapping case involving a brilliant chef and a police commissioner. Each segment showcases Anderson's meticulous visual style at its most elaborate, with compositions so precisely arranged they resemble moving dioramas. The ensemble is staggering — Benicio del Toro, Frances McDormand, Jeffrey Wright, Tilda Swinton, Timothee Chalamet, Bill Murray — each inhabiting their vignettes with the deadpan specificity Anderson's world demands. The story shifts between color and black-and-white, live action and animation, aspect ratios and tonal registers with the restless curiosity of a magazine flipping through its own pages. The emotional texture is characteristically Anderson: controlled surfaces concealing genuine feeling, humor derived from precision rather than chaos. An acquired taste that rewards those who share the director's affection for the particular.

name: Eternals
description: Chloe Zhao brought her indie sensibility to the Marvel Cinematic Universe, directing an action adventure that spans seven thousand years of human history as a group of immortal beings planted on Earth by cosmic Celestials must reunite to face the Deviants and a far more devastating truth about their mission. The ensemble — Gemma Chan, Richard Madden, Kumail Nanjiani, Angelina Jolie, Salma Hayek, and others — represents one of Marvel's most diverse casts, and Zhao films them against real-world landscapes with natural light, giving the science fiction spectacle a grounded, earthy texture unusual for the franchise. The narrative attempts something genuinely ambitious: a meditation on intervention, faith, and whether protecting humanity means controlling it, wrapped inside a superhero framework. The story's scope works both for and against it — the millennia-spanning timeline creates moments of genuine mythic grandeur but also makes certain character arcs feel compressed. The philosophical questions the Eternals face — obedience to a creator versus empathy for the created — carry more weight than most MCU conflicts, even when the action sequences revert to familiar visual-effects spectacle. A polarizing entry that aimed higher than the franchise norm and accepted the risks that come with that ambition.

name: Black Panther: Wakanda Forever
description: Ryan Coogler's sequel carries the immense weight of mourning Chadwick Boseman both within the narrative and beyond it, transforming what could have been a standard superhero follow-up into an action adventure steeped in genuine grief. Letitia Wright steps forward as Shuri, whose journey from reluctant heir to the Black Panther mantle provides the emotional spine of a story that refuses to rush past loss. The introduction of Namor — played by Tenoch Huerta with regal intensity — and the underwater kingdom of Talokan expands the MCU's geography while creating a mirror-image conflict: two hidden civilizations forced into the open by colonial-era exploitation of their resources. Angela Bassett's Queen Ramonda delivers a performance of extraordinary dignity and ferocity, anchoring the political dimensions of the science fiction narrative. The production design remains unmatched in the franchise, blending Afrofuturism with Mesoamerican aesthetics to create visual worlds that feel culturally specific rather than generically fantastical. Ludwig Goransson's score, fusing traditional instrumentation with modern composition, carries emotional weight that dialogue alone cannot. The experience honors its fallen star without making grief its only register, finding room for spectacle, humor, and the complicated business of succession.

name: Deadpool & Wolverine
description: Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman finally share the screen in the way fans demanded for years, with director Shawn Levy orchestrating an action comedy that serves as both a meta-commentary on franchise filmmaking and a genuinely entertaining buddy story. Reynolds' Wade Wilson is pulled from civilian aimlessness into a multiverse-threatening crisis that requires him to team up with a variant of Wolverine — not the noble hero audiences remember, but a broken, guilt-ridden version who failed his world. The science fiction framework allows for an endless parade of cameos and references that reward deep Marvel knowledge, but the emotional core is surprisingly sincere: two men defined by failure learning to care about something again. Jackman brings a physicality and weariness to this Wolverine that distinguishes him from previous iterations, and his chemistry with Reynolds oscillates between genuine hostility and grudging affection in ways that feel earned. The R-rated sensibility — profanity, graphic violence, fourth-wall demolition — remains intact as the character officially enters the MCU, proving the tone can coexist with the larger franchise. Henry Cavill, Jennifer Garner, and Wesley Snipes make appearances that land as both fan service and narrative payoff. Irreverent, self-aware, and more emotionally grounded than it pretends to be.

name: Birds of Prey and the Fantabulous Emancipation of One Harley Quinn
description: Margot Robbie's Harley Quinn breaks free from the Joker's shadow — literally and narratively — in Cathy Yan's action crime story that reimagines Gotham as a neon-drenched playground for a newly single antihero with a violent streak and a craving for breakfast sandwiches. The story weaves together multiple women's paths — Huntress seeking family revenge, Black Canary torn between survival and conscience, Renee Montoya fighting institutional corruption — as they converge around a young pickpocket and a diamond that holds the key to a fortune. Ewan McGregor's Roman Sionis is a scenery-chewing villain whose narcissistic rage provides the antagonistic engine, while the action sequences are staged with John Wick-adjacent brutality and creativity, particularly the funhouse climax at the Booby Trap amusement park. The narrative structure is intentionally messy, told through Harley's unreliable, non-linear perspective, doubling back and correcting itself in ways that mirror her chaotic thought process. The tone is gleefully irreverent without being hollow, and the feminist dimensions feel organic rather than performative — these women do not bond over sisterhood speeches but over shared survival in a city that chews people up. A vivid, violent, candy-colored take on liberation through chaos.

name: The Boy and the Heron
description: Hayao Miyazaki came out of retirement to create what many consider his most personal work — an animated drama fantasy that channels grief, creativity, and the weight of artistic legacy into a story about a boy pulled into a fantastical tower world by a mysterious gray heron. Set during wartime Japan, the narrative follows Mahito as he processes his mother's death while navigating a surreal dimension filled with Miyazaki's signature imagery: vast skies, impossible architecture, creatures that are simultaneously beautiful and unsettling. Studio Ghibli's hand-drawn animation is breathtaking, each frame composed with the painterly precision that has defined the studio for decades. The story resists easy interpretation — it is at once a coming-of-age journey, a meditation on loss, a commentary on creative inheritance, and a farewell from a master who has spent his career building imaginary worlds. The emotional texture is dense and sometimes deliberately opaque, trusting the audience to sit with ambiguity rather than demanding narrative clarity. Joe Hisaishi's score carries enormous emotional weight, guiding the viewer through sequences that operate on dream logic rather than plot mechanics. A profoundly beautiful, deeply strange experience from one of animation's greatest voices.

name: Dune
description: Denis Villeneuve accomplished what decades of Hollywood attempts could not — translating Frank Herbert's dense, philosophical science fiction novel into a cinematic experience that honors the source material's complexity while delivering spectacle of genuinely awe-inspiring scale. Timothee Chalamet plays Paul Atreides with an interiority that makes the character's messianic arc feel more like a burden than a destiny, surrounded by an extraordinary ensemble including Rebecca Ferguson, Oscar Isaac, Josh Brolin, Stellan Skarsgard, and Zendaya. The adventure unfolds on Arrakis, a desert planet whose spice melange drives the galactic economy, and Villeneuve films its landscapes with the reverence of a nature documentarian — vast, indifferent, and terrifyingly beautiful. Hans Zimmer's score pulses with a distinctly non-Western sonic palette, using processed vocals and unfamiliar instrumentation to make the familiar desert setting feel genuinely alien. The pacing is deliberate and unhurried, trusting the audience to absorb political intrigue, ecological themes, and cultural specificity without constant action. The sandworm sequences achieve a sense of sublime terror that justifies the novel's decades-long reputation as unfilmable. Greig Fraser's cinematography renders every frame as a composition worthy of hanging on a wall. An epic that treats intelligence as a feature rather than an obstacle to entertainment.

name: The Trial of the Chicago 7
description: Aaron Sorkin wrote and directed this historical courtroom drama about the infamous trial following the 1968 Democratic National Convention protests, and the result crackles with the verbal velocity and righteous fury that defines his best work. The ensemble — Sacha Baron Cohen as Abbie Hoffman, Eddie Redmayne as Tom Hayden, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as Bobby Seale, Mark Rylance as defense attorney William Kunstler, and Frank Langella as the nakedly biased Judge Julius Hoffman — inhabits a story where the courtroom becomes a theater of political power. The drama operates on dual timescales, cutting between the chaos of the convention and the absurdist proceedings of the trial itself, where the judge's contempt for the defendants is barely disguised. Sorkin's dialogue fires at its characteristic machine-gun pace, but the material earns the intensity — these are men facing years in prison for the crime of organizing dissent. Baron Cohen's Hoffman steals scenes with theatrical defiance, while Abdul-Mateen's Bobby Seale endures treatment so outrageous it would seem fictional if it were not documented history. The story resonates beyond its period setting, its themes of state overreach, protest, and the weaponization of the legal system feeling uncomfortably contemporary.

name: All the Bright Places
description: Elle Fanning and Justice Smith play two teenagers whose chance encounter on a bridge — both contemplating the edge for different reasons — leads to a connection that reshapes both their lives in this drama romance adapted from Jennifer Niven's bestselling young adult novel. The story follows Violet, grieving her sister's death, and Finch, whose erratic brilliance masks a deeper struggle with mental illness, as they embark on a school project exploring the wonders of Indiana. Their road trip discoveries — quirky landmarks, hidden lakes, small-town oddities — serve as scaffolding for conversations about loss, depression, and the difference between being saved and saving yourself. The tone walks a careful line between tenderness and genuine darkness, refusing to treat Finch's condition as a puzzle Violet can solve through love alone. Smith brings a manic energy to Finch that makes his charming moments feel just slightly unstable, while Fanning's Violet carries the quiet weight of someone learning to feel things again. The experience does not shy away from difficult outcomes, and its willingness to sit with pain rather than resolve it neatly gives the story an emotional honesty that distinguishes it from more sanitized young adult fare.

name: Nosferatu
description: Robert Eggers brings his signature historical precision and atmospheric dread to a retelling of the vampire legend, crafting a gothic horror fantasy that treats its source material with the gravity of ancient myth rather than genre convention. Lily-Rose Depp plays Ellen Hutter, a young woman whose psychic connection to the ancient Count Orlok draws darkness toward her household like a plague, and Bill Skarsgard disappears beneath prosthetics and vocal transformation to create a Nosferatu that feels less like a character and more like an elemental force of corruption. The production design is extraordinary — candlelit interiors, fog-shrouded German villages, and shadow work that evokes F.W. Murnau's original while pushing into new territory. Willem Dafoe brings scholarly intensity to Professor Albin Eberhart Von Franz, and Nicholas Hoult grounds the romantic lead with genuine warmth. Eggers treats the vampire not as a seductive figure but as a manifestation of death itself — patient, inevitable, and terrifying in its indifference to human resistance. The pacing is deliberate and dread-soaked, building atmosphere through accumulation rather than jump scares, with Jarin Blaschke's cinematography rendering every frame in textures that feel physically cold. A deeply unsettling, visually ravishing descent into gothic darkness.

name: Rebecca
description: Ben Wheatley directs this adaptation of Daphne du Maurier's classic gothic novel, with Lily James as the unnamed young bride who marries Maxim de Winter — a brooding Armie Hammer — and moves into Manderley, an estate still saturated with the presence of his deceased first wife. The drama mystery romance thriller builds its unease through the architecture of the house itself, its corridors and rooms functioning as extensions of Rebecca's lingering influence. Kristin Scott Thomas delivers an ice-cold performance as Mrs. Danvers, the housekeeper whose devotion to the dead Rebecca transforms from unsettling to genuinely menacing as the story progresses. The narrative operates as a psychological study of inadequacy — the new Mrs. de Winter measuring herself against a phantom she can never match, surrounded by people who seem to prefer the ghost to the living woman. The visual palette shifts from the sunlit warmth of the couple's Mediterranean courtship to the gray, oppressive grandeur of the English estate, mirroring the protagonist's emotional descent. The mystery elements deepen in the second half as secrets about Rebecca's death surface, recontextualizing the entire household's behavior. A gothic atmosphere piece that prioritizes mood and performance over narrative speed.

name: The King's Man
description: Matthew Vaughn takes his Kingsman franchise back to its origins with a prequel set against the backdrop of World War I, following Ralph Fiennes as Orlando Oxford, a pacifist aristocrat forced to assemble a covert network of spies to combat a shadowy cabal orchestrating the war from behind the scenes. The action adventure thriller trades the modern-day cheekiness of the previous entries for something darker and more grounded, though Vaughn's signature style — acrobatic fight choreography, irreverent humor, and stylish excess — still surfaces throughout. The ensemble includes Gemma Arterton, Rhys Ifans as a scene-stealing Rasputin, and Djimon Hounsou, each occupying distinct roles within the proto-Kingsman operation. The Rasputin fight sequence — a poisoning turned knife fight turned dance of death — stands as one of the franchise's best set pieces. The story attempts to balance historical tragedy with genre entertainment, sometimes uneasily, as real events like trench warfare and political assassination share space with cartoonish villainy. Harris Dickinson plays Orlando's son with earnest determination, and the father-son dynamic provides emotional stakes that give the period adventure something personal beneath its spectacle. A tonal experiment that swings ambitiously between gravitas and genre fun.

name: The Empty Man
description: David Prior's directorial debut is a horror mystery that begins as a missing-person investigation and gradually dissolves into something far stranger and more ambitious — a cosmic horror story about tulpas, collective belief, and the terrifying possibility that thought itself can generate reality. James Badge Dale plays an ex-cop searching for a vanished teenager, following a trail that leads from an urban legend about a supernatural entity called The Empty Man to a secretive cult operating out of an isolated compound. The opening prologue — a standalone twenty-minute sequence set in Bhutan — establishes a tone of dread and metaphysical unease that the rest of the story methodically amplifies. The pacing is deliberately slow, trusting the audience to sit with discomfort as the mystery peels back layers that reveal increasingly disturbing implications. The philosophical underpinning draws from Lovecraftian cosmic horror without relying on tentacled creatures, instead locating the terror in the idea that perception shapes existence and that some perceptions, once shared widely enough, become inescapable. The final act recontextualizes the protagonist's entire journey in a way that is genuinely unsettling. Vastly underappreciated on release, the experience has developed a devoted following among horror enthusiasts who prize atmosphere and ideas over jump scares.

name: The Devil All the Time
description: Antonio Campos directed this sprawling, interconnected crime drama thriller set across two decades in the rural hollers of southern Ohio and West Virginia, where violence, corrupt faith, and generational trauma bind together a cast of damaged characters whose paths converge with grim inevitability. Tom Holland leads as Arvin Russell, a young man trying to protect what remains of his family from the predators — human and institutional — that surround them. The ensemble is extraordinary: Robert Pattinson as a lecherous preacher, Bill Skarsgard and Haley Bennett as Arvin's doomed parents, Sebastian Stan and Riley Keough as a serial-killing couple who prey on hitchhikers. Donald Ray Pollock narrates his own novel's adaptation with a Southern Gothic gravity that gives the story the cadence of a dark parable. The tone is relentlessly bleak, building a world where faith is either weaponized or useless, and where the only reliable currency is the capacity for violence. Campos refuses to sentimentalize any of it, letting the brutality land with full weight while finding moments of tenderness between characters who have been given almost no reason to trust anyone. A heavy, masterfully acted ensemble piece about the long shadow of American violence.

name: Black Widow
description: Scarlett Johansson's long-awaited solo outing as Natasha Romanoff arrives as an action adventure set between the events of Civil War and Infinity War, taking the character back to confront the program that made her — the Red Room — and the surrogate family she was forced to leave behind. Director Cate Shortland brings a slightly grittier, more espionage-flavored approach to the MCU formula, with Budapest car chases and safe-house confrontations that owe something to the Bourne series. Florence Pugh steals the experience as Yelena Belova, Natasha's younger sister figure, whose deadpan humor and emotional directness provide both comic relief and the story's most affecting relationship. David Harbour brings lovable absurdity as the Red Guardian, a washed-up Soviet super-soldier clinging to faded glory, while Rachel Weisz grounds the family unit as their scientist mother. The science fiction elements manifest primarily through the villain Taskmaster and the Red Room's mind-control technology, though the story works best in its quieter moments — the dinner table scene where four broken people pretend to be a family they never actually were. The action delivers Marvel's signature scale, but the emotional texture is where the experience finds its identity.

name: Now You See Me: Now You Don't
description: The third installment in the Now You See Me franchise reunites the Horsemen with a new generation of illusionists, pitting Jesse Eisenberg's Daniel Atlas against a diamond heiress running a criminal empire. The crime thriller leans into the series' signature formula of elaborate heists disguised as magic shows, where misdirection operates on both the characters and the audience simultaneously. Jesse Eisenberg and Justice Smith anchor the generational handoff, with the tension between old-guard showmanship and tech-savvy newcomers driving much of the interpersonal drama. The set pieces escalate from intimate card tricks to globe-spanning spectacles, maintaining the franchise's commitment to the idea that the biggest illusion is always the one you did not see coming. The story operates at a brisk pace, layering twist upon twist in a structure designed to keep viewers guessing until the final reveal recontextualizes everything. The ensemble dynamics trade on rivalry and collaboration in equal measure, and the criminal underworld adds genuine menace beneath the playful surface. The franchise has always been about the pleasure of being fooled, and this entry leans fully into that contract — promising that nothing is as it appears while daring the audience to spot the seams.

name: Eurovision Song Contest: The Story of Fire Saga
description: Will Ferrell and Rachel McAdams play Lars and Sigrit, two small-town Icelandic musicians who somehow land a spot representing their country at the Eurovision Song Contest, in a comedy that treats its subject with far more affection than mockery. The music numbers are the story's secret weapon — composed by Savan Kotecha among others, they are legitimately catchy pop productions that could hold their own in an actual Eurovision lineup, particularly the standout "Husavik" which earned an Academy Award nomination. Ferrell's Lars is driven by delusional ambition and a lifelong obsession with winning, while McAdams' Sigrit provides the genuine musical talent and emotional grounding. Dan Stevens nearly derails the entire experience with his gloriously unhinged performance as a flamboyant Russian contestant. Director David Dobkin stages the competition sequences with the over-the-top visual flair Eurovision is famous for — pyrotechnics, elaborate costumes, and staging that treats every performance as an event. The comedy works because it understands that Eurovision's appeal is not ironic distance but sincere commitment to spectacle, and the story mirrors that philosophy. The romance between Lars and Sigrit is gentle and predictable but earns its resolution through accumulated warmth. A love letter disguised as a comedy.

name: Black Adam
description: Dwayne Johnson's long-gestating passion project finally brings the DC antihero to screen, with Jaume Collet-Serra directing an action adventure that positions Teth-Adam as a five-thousand-year-old superpowered figure released into the modern world with a brutally simple approach to justice: kill the bad guys. The science fiction spectacle introduces the nation of Kahndaq, an occupied Middle Eastern country whose people see Adam as a liberator while the Justice Society — Aldis Hodge's Hawkman, Pierce Brosnan's Doctor Fate, Quintessa Swindell's Cyclone, and Noah Centineo's Atom Smasher — sees a threat that needs containment. Johnson's physical presence dominates every frame, and the character's moral simplicity creates genuine friction with heroes accustomed to restraint. Brosnan's Doctor Fate provides the ensemble's emotional anchor, bringing weary gravitas to a sorcerer who has foreseen his own end. The action sequences lean heavily on destruction-level superhero combat — buildings leveled, vehicles hurled, slow-motion lightning strikes — with a visual style that prioritizes spectacle over subtlety. The story grapples with questions of colonial liberation and whether violent resistance is justified, though these themes share space uneasily with blockbuster formula requirements. A vehicle for Johnson's star power wrapped in anti-hero mythology.

name: Extraction
description: Chris Hemsworth trades his Thor hammer for tactical gear in this action thriller from first-time director Sam Hargrave, a former stunt coordinator whose background shows in every frame of the relentlessly physical combat. The story drops Tyler Rake, a burnt-out mercenary with a death wish, into Dhaka, Bangladesh, where he must extract the kidnapped son of an imprisoned drug lord — a straightforward premise that serves as scaffolding for some of the most impressive action choreography in recent memory. The centerpiece is a twelve-minute faux-single-take sequence that moves through apartment buildings, streets, and vehicles with breathless fluidity, blending practical stunt work with seamless digital stitching. Hemsworth brings genuine physicality and a quiet sadness to Rake, whose recklessness reads as suicidal grief rather than invincibility. Joe Russo produced and co-wrote the screenplay, bringing a producer's understanding of how to stage large-scale action on a Netflix budget. The Dhaka setting provides a dense, chaotic urban environment that the story uses to maximum tactical advantage — rooftop chases, market shootouts, and bridge standoffs that feel genuinely dangerous. The emotional depth is modest but sufficient, giving the relentless action just enough human weight to land. A pure combat experience executed at the highest level.

name: Maestro
description: Bradley Cooper directed, co-wrote, and stars as Leonard Bernstein in this drama romance that is less a biographical survey of the legendary composer-conductor's career than an intimate portrait of his marriage to Felicia Montealegre, played with luminous intensity by Carey Mulligan. The experience spans decades, shifting between black-and-white and color cinematography to mirror different emotional registers in the couple's life together. Cooper's physical transformation is remarkable — prosthetics, movement, and vocal cadence create a Bernstein who ages across the story with convincing specificity — but the performance lives in the character's restless, contradictory energy: a man who conducts orchestras with total authority yet cannot conduct his own emotional life with any consistency. Mulligan's Felicia is the revelation, bringing dignity and barely suppressed anguish to a woman who chose to love someone whose attention was always fractured between art, ambition, and other relationships. The music sequences, particularly a cathedral conducting scene, are staged with thrilling visual imagination, and the sound design places the audience inside the experience of creating rather than merely witnessing it. The story does not resolve the contradictions of Bernstein's life — it presents them as the fabric of the marriage itself. A sweeping, deeply felt exploration of love sustained through fundamental incompatibility.

name: The Good Nurse
description: Jessica Chastain and Eddie Redmayne deliver restrained, deeply unsettling performances in this crime drama mystery based on the true story of Charles Cullen, a nurse who killed patients at multiple hospitals over sixteen years while the healthcare system repeatedly failed to stop him. Chastain plays Amy Loughren, a single mother and nurse struggling with a serious heart condition, whose genuine friendship with Cullen makes her eventual role in his capture both heroic and heartbreaking. Director Tobias Lindholm strips away procedural theatrics in favor of quiet dread — the horror here is institutional, residing in hospitals that transferred a suspected killer rather than reporting him because liability mattered more than lives. Redmayne plays Cullen with unnerving normality, a man whose kindness to colleagues coexists with something profoundly broken, and the story never asks the audience to understand his psychology — only to witness the system that enabled it. The investigation by two dogged detectives, played by Nnamdi Asomugha and Noah Emmerich, provides the procedural throughline, but the emotional weight rests entirely on Chastain's Amy and the impossible position of suspecting someone you care about. A true-crime story more interested in complicity than sensationalism.

name: Zola
description: Janicza Bravo directed this comedy crime drama based on A'Ziah "Zola" King's legendary 2015 Twitter thread — a 148-tweet saga about a road trip to Florida that spirals from exotic dancing into trafficking, violence, and surreal chaos. Taylour Paige plays Zola with cool, observational detachment, narrating her descent into someone else's nightmare with the sardonic clarity of the original tweets. Riley Keough is electric as Stefani, the white woman whose manipulative friendliness masks something far more desperate and dangerous, and their dynamic captures a specific kind of toxic female friendship built on mutual exploitation. Colman Domingo's presence as a pimp adds genuine menace to a story that might otherwise tip into pure absurdity. Bravo's visual style is inventive and deliberately disorienting — social media notification sounds punctuate scenes, the camera lingers on details that emphasize the transactional nature of every interaction, and the pacing mimics the addictive scroll of the thread itself. The story occupies an uncomfortable space between comedy and horror, finding dark humor in exploitation without diminishing its real consequences. The Florida setting is rendered as a neon-soaked purgatory where everyone is performing a version of themselves for an audience they cannot see.

name: The Courier
description: Benedict Cumberbatch stars as Greville Wynne, an unassuming British businessman recruited by MI6 and the CIA to serve as a courier for Oleg Penkovsky, a Soviet military intelligence officer providing secrets that would prove critical during the Cuban Missile Crisis. The drama history thriller is built on the contrast between Wynne's ordinariness and the extraordinary danger he walks into — a man with no training, no ideology, and no particular courage who gradually develops all three through the relationship he forms with his Soviet contact, played with quiet intensity by Merab Ninidze. Director Dominic Cooke maintains a measured, restrained tone that prioritizes human connection over spy-thriller mechanics, allowing the friendship between Wynne and Penkovsky to carry the emotional weight. Cumberbatch's physical transformation in the story's later stages — depicting Wynne's imprisonment and deterioration — is genuinely harrowing. The period detail is precise without being showy, and the Cold War paranoia builds through accumulation of small, tense moments rather than action set pieces. The story resonates as a portrait of ordinary courage — the kind that does not announce itself but simply refuses to look away when looking away would be easier and safer.

name: The Willoughbys
description: This animated adventure comedy takes the darkly whimsical premise of Lois Lowry's children's book — four siblings who scheme to get rid of their terrible parents — and renders it in a distinctive visual style that looks like felt and yarn brought to life. The Willoughby children, led by eldest brother Tim and voiced by Will Forte, Maya Rudolph, Alessia Cara, and others, hatch an elaborate plan to send their neglectful parents on a vacation from which they will hopefully never return. The humor runs darker than typical family fare, treating parental abandonment as a launching point for a story about what family actually means when the one you were born into fails you. The animation style from Bron Studios is deliberately textured and tactile, creating a world that feels handcrafted in a way that contrasts pleasantly with the smooth digital polish of most contemporary animation. Ricky Gervais narrates as the family cat with characteristic dryness. The fantasy elements manifest through the story's heightened reality — an orphan-factory run by a candy-coated nanny, a commander-in-chief voiced by Terry Crews — while the emotional core stays grounded in recognizably real feelings of rejection and resilience.

name: Killers of the Flower Moon
description: Martin Scorsese's epic crime drama history unfolds across three and a half hours in 1920s Oklahoma, where the Osage Nation — sitting atop the richest oil deposits in the world — is systematically murdered by white settlers orchestrating a campaign of terror disguised as marriage and friendship. Leonardo DiCaprio plays Ernest Burkhart, a weak, greedy man who genuinely loves his Osage wife Mollie, played by Lily Gladstone, while simultaneously participating in the conspiracy orchestrated by his uncle William Hale, a chillingly avuncular Robert De Niro. Gladstone's performance is the quiet center of the experience — her Mollie watches her family die around her with a grief that is oceanic in its depth and devastating in its restraint. Scorsese refuses to make the story a conventional detective procedural, instead forcing the audience to sit with the perpetrators' perspective and recognize how ordinary evil looks when it operates in broad daylight. The cinematography by Rodrigo Prieto renders the Oklahoma landscape as both beautiful and blood-soaked. Jesse Plemons arrives late as an FBI investigator, but the story's power lies in the long, uncomfortable hours before anyone in authority thought Osage lives were worth investigating. A masterwork of American reckoning.

name: Cruella
description: Emma Stone plays the young Cruella de Vil in a comedy crime drama origin story set against the punk rock explosion of 1970s London, reimagining the iconic Disney villain as a scrappy, orphaned fashion genius waging war against the Baroness, an established couturier played with imperious menace by Emma Thompson. Director Craig Gillespie leans heavily into the visual possibilities of the fashion world, staging confrontations as design battles where each outfit is a weapon and every gala is a battlefield. The costume design by Jenny Beavan is genuinely spectacular — a garbage truck dress, a Dalmatian-themed gown that emerges from flames — and functions as the story's primary language for expressing identity, rage, and ambition. Stone's Estella-to-Cruella transformation charts a course from sympathetic underdog to something more morally complicated, while Thompson's Baroness provides the kind of formidable antagonist who makes the protagonist's descent feel earned rather than arbitrary. The 1970s London setting is rendered with period-accurate music — The Clash, Blondie, The Doors — and production design that makes the city feel both gritty and glamorous. The crime elements involve elaborate heists and public provocations that treat fashion as guerrilla warfare. A visually intoxicating villain origin that takes genuine pleasure in its own audacity.

name: The Lodge
description: Directors Severin Fiala and Veronika Franz craft a slow-burn horror thriller set almost entirely within a snowbound lodge where a father's new girlfriend — a survivor of a religious cult's mass suicide — is left alone with his two resentful children over the holidays. Riley Keough plays Grace with a fragile composure that the story methodically dismantles, as inexplicable events begin eroding her grip on reality: belongings vanish, the power fails, and religious imagery from her traumatic past starts appearing where it should not be. The drama mystery operates in the space between psychological deterioration and something genuinely supernatural, refusing to commit to either explanation until its devastating final act. The children, played by Jaeden Martell and Lia McHugh, bring an unsettling stillness to their performances — their grief over their mother's suicide and their hostility toward Grace creating an atmosphere of domestic tension that the horror elements amplify rather than replace. The cinematography by Thimios Bakatakis emphasizes isolation through vast white landscapes and claustrophobic interior framing. The pacing demands patience, building dread through accumulation of small wrongnesses rather than jump scares. The resolution is genuinely disturbing, recontextualizing everything with a cruelty that lingers long after the story ends.

name: West Side Story
description: Steven Spielberg's lifelong dream of directing a musical resulted in a reimagining of the Bernstein and Sondheim classic that feels both reverential and vitally alive, staging the Romeo and Juliet-inspired crime drama romance in a 1950s New York that is being literally demolished around its characters. Rachel Zegler and Ansel Elgort play Maria and Tony, but the real revelation is Ariana DeBose's Anita, whose performance earned a deserved Academy Award — fierce, joyful, and ultimately heartbreaking. Spielberg's camera work during the dance numbers is extraordinary, moving through space with a fluidity and energy that makes the choreography feel spontaneous rather than staged. The production design by Adam Stockhausen renders the West Side as a neighborhood caught between destruction and community, with demolition sites and tenement rooftops serving as stages for both violence and romance. Rita Moreno, who played Anita in the original, returns in a newly created role that adds emotional depth and generational perspective. The musical score, performed by the New York Philharmonic under Gustavo Dudamel, thunders with orchestral power. The story's tragic architecture remains intact, and Spielberg's direction ensures the violence that underpins the gang rivalry lands with genuine weight rather than choreographed elegance.

name: Happiest Season
description: Clea DuVall wrote and directed this holiday comedy romance about Abby, played by Kristen Stewart, who plans to propose to her girlfriend Harper, played by Mackenzie Davis, during the family's Christmas gathering — only to discover that Harper has not come out to her conservative parents. The premise takes the familiar holiday-homecoming formula and filters it through a specifically queer experience, where the tension is not merely social awkwardness but the fundamental question of whether someone you love is ashamed of who you are. Stewart plays Abby's mounting frustration and hurt with quiet intensity, while Davis captures the impossible position of someone torn between the family she was born into and the life she has chosen. Dan Levy delivers the standout supporting performance as Abby's best friend, whose monologue about coming out provides the story's most emotionally direct moment. The ensemble — including Alison Brie as a competitive sister and Mary Steenburgen as the appearance-obsessed mother — creates a household where surface perfection masks genuine dysfunction. The comedy works best when exploring the specific indignities of being closeted in your own family's home, and the romance earns its resolution by taking the characters' pain seriously before arriving at warmth.

name: Guillermo del Toro's Pinocchio
description: Guillermo del Toro reimagines the Pinocchio story through stop-motion animation set against the rise of fascism in 1930s Italy, transforming a children's fable into a meditation on obedience, mortality, and what makes life worth living. The adventure drama fantasy eschews Disney's sanitized version entirely, returning to the story's darker roots while adding del Toro's characteristic fascination with monsters, death, and the intersection of the sacred and the profane. The puppet Pinocchio — voiced with irrepressible energy by Gregory Mann — is not a disobedient boy who needs to learn compliance but a wild, questioning spirit whose refusal to conform is presented as a virtue in a world demanding blind loyalty to authority. Ewan McGregor voices Sebastian J. Cricket with weary, affectionate narration, and the supporting cast includes Christoph Waltz, Tilda Swinton, and Cate Blanchett. The stop-motion animation is breathtaking — each frame handcrafted with a tactile warmth that makes the wooden characters feel more alive than many digital creations. The story directly confronts death in ways that are surprising for the genre, with Pinocchio's immortality becoming a source of both comedy and profound sadness. The emotional climax is earned through genuine philosophical weight rather than sentimental manipulation. A masterwork of animated storytelling.

name: Pinocchio
description: Robert Zemeckis directs this Disney live-action reimagining of their animated classic, with Tom Hanks as Geppetto and a digitally rendered Pinocchio brought to life through CGI and motion capture. The adventure family fantasy follows familiar beats — the Blue Fairy, Honest John, Pleasure Island, the whale — blending practical sets with digital characters to bridge nostalgia and modern techniques. Hanks brings warmth to Geppetto, leaning toward gentleness rather than the comic desperation of the original character. Benjamin Evan Ainsworth voices Pinocchio with earnest sincerity, and the supporting cast includes Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Jiminy Cricket, Cynthia Erivo as the Blue Fairy, and Luke Evans as a menacing Coachman. The production design recreates the Italian village setting with fairy-tale detail, and the Pleasure Island sequence updates the original's cautionary elements for a contemporary audience. Fabiana, a new character performed by Kyanne Lamaya, provides a thematic mirror to Pinocchio's quest for autonomy through her puppeteer artistry. The experience is faithful to its source material, though the additions feel modest against the template's familiarity. A lovingly crafted retelling that struggles to justify itself alongside its animated predecessor.

name: Being the Ricardos
description: Aaron Sorkin writes and directs a drama history that compresses the crisis points of Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz's marriage and career into a single production week of I Love Lucy, when communist accusations, tabloid revelations, and creative disagreements all collide simultaneously. Nicole Kidman plays Lucy with steely intelligence and perfectionist intensity, capturing the mind behind the comedy rather than attempting a physical impersonation, while Javier Bardem's Desi brings charismatic warmth undercut by the strain of being perpetually underestimated. The story operates on multiple timescales — the frantic present of the production week, flashbacks to the couple's courtship and early career, and interview segments from cast and crew members reflecting decades later. Sorkin's signature dialogue crackles throughout, particularly in scenes where Lucy argues blocking and staging with the writers' room, revealing a woman whose comic genius was inseparable from her need for control. J.K. Simmons and Nina Arianda provide excellent support as William Frawley and Vivian Vance, whose off-screen tensions mirror the central couple's struggles. The experience illuminates how the most beloved comedy on television was produced by people whose real lives were anything but funny. A sharp, well-acted portrait of partnership under pressure.

name: Wolfwalkers
description: Cartoon Saloon's animated adventure fantasy is a visual masterpiece that uses hand-drawn animation inspired by medieval woodcuts to tell a story set in 1650s Kilkenny, Ireland, where a young English hunter named Robyn befriends Mebh, a wild girl who belongs to a legendary tribe of wolfwalkers — humans who become wolves when they sleep. The animation style is genuinely unlike anything else in contemporary cinema: flat, angular, and luminous, with the forest rendered in swirling organic lines that contrast with the rigid geometric patterns of the walled town. The story operates as both a fairy tale and a political allegory, with Oliver Cromwell's colonization of Ireland providing the historical backdrop for a narrative about fear of the wild, suppression of native culture, and the violence that follows when empires demand conformity. Honor Kneafsey voices Mebh with infectious, untamed energy, and the family-friendly surface conceals genuinely complex themes about freedom, identity, and the cost of civilization's expansion. The score by Bruno Coulais and Kila blends traditional Irish instrumentation with orchestral grandeur. Tomm Moore and Ross Stewart direct with a visual imagination that makes every frame feel like a page from an illuminated manuscript come to life.

name: Guns Akimbo
description: Daniel Radcliffe plays Miles, a meek online troll who wakes up with guns literally bolted to both hands after antagonizing the wrong person on the internet, forced to compete in Skizm — an underground gladiatorial death match live-streamed to bloodthirsty audiences worldwide. Director Jason Lei Howden builds an action comedy crime thriller around this absurd premise with the frantic energy of a video game set to punk rock, leaning into hyperviolent slapstick as Miles stumbles through increasingly desperate situations while trying to survive against Nix, a genuinely dangerous combatant played with feral intensity by Samara Weaving. The satire of internet culture and violence-as-entertainment is painted in broad, neon-colored strokes rather than subtle commentary, but the kinetic energy and Radcliffe's committed physical comedy keep the experience moving at a pace that never allows boredom. The visual style borrows liberally from Edgar Wright's rapid editing and Scott Pilgrim's graphic-novel aesthetics, creating a world where everything operates at maximum volume. Weaving's Nix is the standout — a killing machine whose backstory adds unexpected pathos beneath the mayhem. The story works best as pure adrenaline delivery, a sugar-rush of absurdist violence for audiences who enjoy their action drenched in dark comedy and self-aware excess.

name: I'm Thinking of Ending Things
description: Charlie Kaufman adapts Iain Reid's novel into a drama mystery thriller that operates less as a conventional narrative and more as an experience of cognitive dissolution, following a young woman — played by Jessie Buckley with anxious, shifting intelligence — as she accompanies her boyfriend Jake to visit his parents on a remote farm during a snowstorm. Nothing is stable: her name changes, her profession shifts between scenes, the parents played by Toni Collette and David Thewlis appear at different ages without explanation, and the timeline folds in on itself with deliberate, disorienting purpose. Kaufman uses the surface-level road trip structure as scaffolding for a meditation on memory, regret, aging, and the stories we construct to make sense of lives that resist coherent narration. The tone is deeply unsettling without relying on horror conventions — the dread comes from the growing sense that reality itself is unreliable and that the narrator may not exist in the way the audience assumes. Jesse Plemons brings a wounded intensity to Jake, whose connection to the mysterious school janitor who appears in intercut scenes provides the story's most heartbreaking revelation. Dense, demanding, and deliberately alienating, the experience rewards those willing to surrender to its fractured logic.

name: A Quiet Place Part II
description: John Krasinski returns to write and direct this horror science fiction thriller sequel that expands the world beyond the Abbott family farm, following the survivors as they venture into territory where sound-hunting alien creatures are not the only threat. Emily Blunt anchors the story with the same fierce maternal intensity that defined the original, but this entry shifts focus toward the children — Millicent Simmonds' Regan, whose deafness provides both survival advantage and the key to fighting back, and Noah Jupe's Marcus, who must overcome paralyzing fear to protect his family. Cillian Murphy joins as Emmett, a grief-hollowed neighbor whose reluctant partnership with Regan provides the story's most compelling dynamic. Krasinski demonstrates exceptional control of tension, using silence as a weapon with the same effectiveness as the first entry while expanding the sonic landscape to include new environments — a dock, a foundry, a feral island community. The opening prologue — depicting the first day of the alien invasion — is a masterful sequence of escalating chaos that contextualizes the entire franchise. The pacing is relentless once the story splits into parallel survival tracks, crosscutting between threats with precision. A sequel that honors its predecessor's discipline while justifying its expanded scope.

name: Fantasy Island
description: Jeff Wadlow directs this Blumhouse reimagining of the classic television series as an adventure fantasy horror mystery, where a group of contest winners arrives at a luxurious tropical resort promising to make their deepest fantasies come true — only to discover that the island's magic operates on rules that twist every wish into something dangerous. Michael Pena plays Mr. Roarke, the enigmatic host, with a calm authority that conceals the island's darker purposes. The ensemble of guests each brings a different desire — revenge, adventure, reunion with lost loved ones — and the story follows each fantasy as it curdles from dream to nightmare. The premise has genuine potential for Twilight Zone-style irony, and the tropical setting provides an effective contrast between paradise surfaces and the horror lurking beneath. The tonal balance is the story's primary challenge, as it attempts to service horror, comedy, mystery, and emotional drama simultaneously. The interconnected structure reveals how the guests' fantasies overlap in unexpected ways, building toward a final twist that recontextualizes their connections. Lucy Hale, Maggie Q, and Austin Stowell anchor their respective storylines with varying effectiveness. A horror-tinged take on wish fulfillment that works best when leaning into its Rod Serling-inspired morality-play roots.

name: The First Omen
description: Arkasha Stevenson's directorial debut serves as a prequel to the legendary Omen franchise, tracing the events leading to the birth of the Antichrist through the eyes of a young American nun named Margaret, played with fierce conviction by Nell Tiger Free. Set in Rome during a period of religious upheaval, the horror story builds its dread through the institutional corruption of the Catholic Church — the conspiracy here is not external but embedded within the walls of the convent itself. The production design drenches every frame in religious iconography that feels simultaneously sacred and threatening, with candlelit corridors and stone interiors creating an atmosphere of claustrophobic devotion. Stevenson demonstrates remarkable control of tone, favoring sustained unease and body horror over the jump scares that have plagued modern franchise horror, with several sequences that push the boundaries of the genre in genuinely shocking directions. Bill Nighy brings gravitas to a cardinal whose role in the conspiracy adds institutional weight to the supernatural elements. The story treats Margaret's faith as both her vulnerability and her weapon, and Free's performance captures the specific terror of discovering that the institution you trusted with your soul has been working against it. Deeply atmospheric and bracingly committed to its own darkness.

name: Everything Everywhere All at Once
description: Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert — the Daniels — created something that should not work: an action adventure science fiction story about a Chinese-American laundromat owner who discovers she can access the skills and memories of her alternate-universe selves while being audited by the IRS. Michelle Yeoh delivers a career-defining performance as Evelyn Wang, a woman whose life has been defined by disappointment — a strained marriage to Ke Huy Quan's gentle Waymond, a disapproving father, and a daughter whose queerness she cannot accept. The multiverse mechanics serve as both visual spectacle and emotional metaphor, with each alternate reality representing a path not taken and the cumulative weight of all those unlived lives becoming the story's central philosophical concern. Ke Huy Quan's comeback performance is extraordinary — his Waymond's quiet insistence that kindness is not weakness provides the story's moral center. Stephanie Hsu's Joy/Jobu Tupaki embodies nihilistic despair with frightening conviction. The experience oscillates between absurdist comedy — hot dog fingers, a raccoon controlling a chef — and moments of devastating emotional clarity, and the tonal shifts feel earned because the Daniels understand that absurdity and sincerity are not opposites but neighbors. A generational experience about choosing love in a meaningless universe.

name: Evangelion: 3.0+1.0 Thrice Upon a Time
description: Hideaki Anno's final Rebuild of Evangelion brings the saga that began in 1995 to a conclusion that is simultaneously a spectacular action animation, a deeply personal psychological drama, and a love letter from a creator to the characters and fans who have accompanied him through decades of depression and artistic struggle. The science fiction narrative picks up in a devastated world where the few remaining humans cling to existence, but the story's true battleground is internal — Shinji Ikari's paralysis, Gendo's obsessive grief, and the question of whether people who have been broken by loss can choose to move forward. Studio Khara's animation reaches extraordinary heights, blending hand-drawn warmth with CGI spectacle in battle sequences that are both visually overwhelming and emotionally resonant. Anno treats the franchise's mythology — Angels, Instrumentality, the Human Instrumentality Project — not as lore to be explained but as metaphor for the human desire to dissolve boundaries between self and other. The resolution is surprisingly warm and hopeful, a genuine departure for a series defined by psychological anguish, and it reads as Anno's own act of healing — letting go of the story that consumed him. A definitive ending to one of animation's most important sagas.

name: Without Remorse
description: Michael B. Jordan stars as John Clark, Tom Clancy's iconic operative, in an action thriller war story that follows a Navy SEAL whose pregnant wife is murdered as part of a conspiracy reaching into the highest levels of American and Russian intelligence. Director Stefano Sollima brings a grounded, tactical approach to the combat sequences, staging them with the kind of close-quarters intensity that emphasizes the physical reality of violence rather than romanticizing it. Jordan's physicality is formidable — his Clark operates with a controlled fury that makes the character's single-minded pursuit of vengeance feel genuinely dangerous rather than heroically sanitized. The story moves from domestic tragedy through covert operations in Syria and Russia, building toward revelations about how governments sacrifice individuals to maintain geopolitical balance. Jamie Bell plays a CIA operative whose motivations remain deliberately opaque, and Jodie Turner-Smith brings authority to a fellow SEAL whose loyalty to Clark provides the story's most reliable human connection. The Clancy universe's hallmarks — military procedure, intelligence tradecraft, and the moral compromises of statecraft — provide the framework, though the experience prioritizes visceral action over the source material's more cerebral political analysis. A vehicle for Jordan's intensity that delivers efficient, brutal genre satisfaction.

name: The Little Mermaid
description: Disney's live-action reimagining of their beloved animated classic casts Halle Bailey as Ariel, and her performance immediately justifies the adaptation — a voice of extraordinary range and emotional expressiveness paired with a wide-eyed wonder that makes the character's fascination with the human world feel genuine rather than naive. Director Rob Marshall stages the underwater sequences with vibrant color and flowing choreography, though the transition between oceanic and terrestrial settings highlights the contrast between digital spectacle and practical filmmaking. Melissa McCarthy brings theatrical menace and dark humor to Ursula, the sea witch whose bargain drives the adventure family fantasy romance, while Daveed Diggs, Awkwafina, and Jacob Tremblay voice Ariel's marine companions with contemporary energy. The Alan Menken score retains its iconic songs — "Part of Your World" and "Under the Sea" — while adding new compositions by Menken and Lin-Manuel Miranda that expand the emotional palette. Jonah Hauer-King's Prince Eric is given more depth and agency than his animated counterpart, and his chemistry with Bailey makes the romance feel mutual rather than one-sided. The story's themes of curiosity, sacrifice, and the desire to belong somewhere larger than your origins carry forward with sincerity. A lavish retelling anchored by a star-making central performance.

name: Roald Dahl's The Witches
description: Robert Zemeckis directs this adaptation of Roald Dahl's darkly comic children's story, relocating the setting from England to 1960s Alabama and casting Octavia Spencer as the boy's resourceful grandmother. The comedy family fantasy horror follows a young orphan who stumbles upon a convention of witches at a seaside hotel, led by the Grand High Witch — Anne Hathaway in a performance of gleeful, scenery-devouring menace that embraces the grotesque with visible delight. Hathaway's exaggerated facial expressions and physical transformation provide the experience's most entertaining element, turning the villain into a figure simultaneously terrifying and hilarious. The production design renders the hotel setting with period charm, and the witch transformation effects — elongated limbs, split mouths, clawed hands — aim for the body horror that made Dahl's original so memorably unsettling for young readers. Spencer's grandmother brings warmth and cultural specificity to a role that grounds the fantasy in real-world knowledge about evil and resilience. The relocation to Alabama adds racial dimension to themes of persecution and survival. Stanley Tucci adds comic grace as the hotel manager. A visually inventive adaptation buoyed by Hathaway's commitment to the absurd.

name: The Many Saints of Newark
description: David Chase returns to the world of The Sopranos with a crime drama prequel set during the Newark riots of 1967, following Dickie Moltisanti — played by Alessandro Nivola — the mentor and father figure whose shadow loomed large over the original series. Michael Gandolfini steps into the role of young Tony Soprano with an uncanny physical and vocal resemblance to his late father James Gandolfini, giving the few scenes he occupies an emotional weight that transcends the screen. The story traces the intersecting pressures of organized crime, racial tension, and family loyalty as Newark's Italian and Black communities collide during a period of genuine historical upheaval. Nivola's Dickie is charismatic and violent in equal measure, a man whose mentorship of young Tony plants seeds the audience knows will grow into something destructive. Vera Farmiga plays Livia Soprano with the controlled bitterness that fans will recognize as the foundation for one of television's most memorable characters. The Newark setting provides a grittier, more politically charged backdrop than the suburban New Jersey of the series, though the story's attempts to service multiple timelines and character introductions occasionally fragment its focus. A companion piece that enriches the original rather than replacing it.

name: The Dry
description: Eric Bana returns to Australian cinema as Aaron Falk, a federal police officer who comes back to his drought-stricken rural hometown for a funeral and finds himself drawn into reinvestigating a decades-old case that drove him away in the first place. The crime mystery thriller, based on Jane Harper's bestselling novel, uses the oppressive Australian heat as both setting and metaphor — the landscape is parched, cracked, and unforgiving, mirroring a community where old resentments and buried secrets fester beneath a surface of small-town familiarity. Director Robert Connolly builds tension through dual timelines, intercutting between the present investigation and flashbacks to a teenage tragedy that left one girl dead and the town divided over who was responsible. Bana brings a quiet, weary authority to Falk, whose return stirs suspicions and hostilities that most people would prefer stayed dormant. The pacing is deliberately measured, allowing the heat and isolation to become characters in their own right, and the mystery unfolds through conversation and observation rather than dramatic confrontation. The Australian rural landscape is photographed with harsh, beautiful clarity, making the environment feel simultaneously vast and suffocating. A taut, atmospheric investigation where the past refuses to stay buried.

name: Soul
description: Pixar's most philosophically ambitious work follows Joe Gardner, a middle-school music teacher voiced by Jamie Foxx, who finally gets his big break as a jazz pianist — then falls down a manhole and finds himself in the Great Before, where unborn souls develop their personalities before heading to Earth. The animated drama family fantasy music experience pairs Joe with 22, a cynical soul voiced by Tina Fey who has refused to find her "spark" for millennia, and their journey together becomes a meditation on whether purpose is something you discover or something you choose. Pete Docter and Kemp Powers direct with Pixar's characteristic emotional intelligence, but the visual design pushes into genuinely new territory — the Great Before rendered as abstract, geometric spaces of soft light, while New York City is depicted with textured detail that celebrates Black culture, jazz clubs, and barbershops with loving specificity. Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross provide the ethereal afterlife score while Jon Batiste delivers the jazz compositions. The emotional climax arrives not through dramatic revelation but through a quiet moment of awareness — the recognition that a life well-lived is made of ordinary moments savored.

name: Space Jam: A New Legacy
description: LeBron James steps into the role Michael Jordan made iconic, teaming up with the Looney Tunes in an adventure animation comedy that doubles as a sprawling advertisement for Warner Bros.' intellectual property catalog. The story sends LeBron and his son Dom into the Warner Bros. Serververse, a digital realm controlled by a rogue AI played by Don Cheadle, where the only way to escape is winning a basketball game against algorithmically enhanced opponents. The Looney Tunes — Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, and the full roster — appear in various Warner properties from Mad Max to The Matrix to Harry Potter, creating a visual spectacle that is part basketball spectacle, part corporate Easter-egg hunt. The science fiction family framework exists primarily to justify these crossover moments, and the animated sequences deliver the chaotic energy the Looney Tunes are known for. LeBron's acting is earnest and self-deprecating, and the father-son relationship provides a genuine emotional throughline about respecting children's choices rather than projecting your own ambitions onto them. The basketball game itself is inventively staged, blending cartoon physics with athletic spectacle. The experience works best as pure sensory overload for younger audiences and nostalgia delivery for older ones.

name: Onward
description: Pixar blends fantasy world-building with suburban mundanity in an animated adventure comedy about two elf brothers — voiced by Tom Holland and Chris Pratt — who receive a magical staff that can bring their deceased father back for one day, only for the spell to go wrong and produce only his lower half. The quest to complete the spell before time runs out drives a road trip through a world where mythical creatures have traded magic for technology, centaurs ride motorcycles instead of galloping, and a manticore runs a family restaurant instead of a dungeon. The comedy mines this juxtaposition effectively, finding humor in pixies who have become biker gangs and unicorns who rummage through garbage. But the emotional core is bracingly real: Ian, the younger brother who never met his father, must reckon with the possibility that the person he has been missing all along was standing right next to him. The family fantasy wraps fraternal love in genre trappings that make its emotional conclusions feel earned rather than sentimental.
